passages.source_text: Τετάρτῃ δὲ ἡμέρᾳ τῆς ἐν Τύρῳ ἡμῶν ἐπιδημίας ὑπὸ τὸν ὄρθρον προεληλυθότι τῷ Πέτρῳ ἀπήντων πλησιόχωροί τε οὐκ ὀλίγοι καὶ αὐτῆς Τύρου πάνπολλοι καὶ ἐπεφώνουν λέγοντες Ὁ θεὸς διὰ σοῦ ἡμᾶς ἐλεείτω, διὰ σοῦ θεραπευέτω. ὁ δὲ Πέτρος ἔστη ἐπὶ λίθου τινὸς ὑψηλοῦ πρὸς τὸ δύνασθαι πᾶσιν ὁρᾶσθαι, καὶ προσαγορεύσας θεοσεβεῖ νόμῳ οὕτως ἤρξατο·

Θεῷ τῷ κτίσαντι τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὸ σύμπαν οὐ λείπει πρόφασις πρὸς σωτηρίαν τῶν σώζεσθαι θελόντων. ὅθεν μηδὲ ἐπὶ τοῖς δοκοῦσιν φαύλοις ὑπὸ προπετείας τις αὐτὸν ὡς μὴ φιλάνθρωπον αἰτιάσθω. τῶν γὰρ συμβαινόντων ἀνθρώπῳ τὰ τέλη ἀνθρώποις μὲν ἄγνωστα, ὡς ἐπὶ κακῷ ὑποπτευόμενα, θεῷ δὲ ὡς ἀποβησόμενα εὐτυχῶς γνώριμα. αὐτίκα γοῦν Σίμων ἀριστερὰ τοῦ θεοῦ δύναμις ὢν καὶ τῶν τὸν θεὸν οὐκ εἰδότων ἐπὶ κακοποιΐᾳ τὴν ἐξουσίαν ἔχων νόσοις ὑμᾶς περιβαλεῖν ἠδυνήθη, αἵτινες διὰ τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ ἀγαθὴν πρόνοιαν γενέσθαι συγχωρηθεῖσαι ἠνάγκασαν ὑμᾶς, τὸν ἰᾶσθαι δυνάμενον περιβλεψαμένους καὶ εὑρόντας, προφάσει τῆς τοῦ σώματος θεραπείας τὰ θεῷ δοκοῦντα ἀναδεξαμένους πεισθῆναι φρονεῖν, ἵνα οὕτως ἅμα τοῖς σώμασι σωθησομένοις καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς σώας ἔχητε.

μανθάνω οὖν ὡς βουθυτήσας εἱστίασεν ὑμᾶς ἐν μέσῃ τῇ ἀγορᾷ καὶ οὕτως ὑμεῖς οἴνῳ πολλῷ παρενεχθέντες ἅμα τοῖς πονηροῖς δαίμοσιν τὸν ἄρχοντα αὐτῶν ἐφιλοφρονεῖσθε καὶ οὕτως ὑμῶν οἱ πλεῖστοι ὑπὸ τῶν παθῶν κατελήφθησαν, ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ καθ’ ἑαυτῶν ἰδίαις χερσὶν ἐπισπασάμενοι τὸ τοῦ ὀλέθρου ξίφος. οὐ γὰρ ἂν τὴν καθ’ ὑμῶν ἔσχον ἐξουσίαν οἱ δαίμονες, εἰ μὴ πρότερον τῷ ἄρχοντι αὐτῶν ὁμοδίαιτοι ἐγεγόνειτε. οὗτος γὰρ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ὑπὸ τοῦ πάντα κτίσαντος θεοῦ δυσὶν ἑκάστοτε ἄρχουσι, δεξιῶν τε καὶ εὐωνύμων, ὡρίσθη νόμος, μὴ ἔχειν ἑκάτερον αὐτῶν ἐξουσίαν, ἐὰν μὴ πρότερόν τινι ὁμοτράπεζος γένηται, ὃν εὖ ποιῆσαι ἢ κακῶσαι βούλεται. ὥσπερ οὖν τῶν δαίμοσιν ἀποδεδομένων θυμάτων μεταλαβόντες τῷ τῆς κακίας ἡγεμόνι κατεδουλώθητε, οὕτως, ἂν τούτων παυσάμενοι τῷ θεῷ διὰ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ καὶ δεξιοῦ ἡγεμόνος προσφύγητε, ·ἀθύτοις τιμαῖς ποιοῦντες ἃ βούλεται, εὖ ἴστε ὅτι σὺν τῇ τοῦ σώματος ἰάσει καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ὑγιαινούσας ἕξετε. αὐτὸς γὰρ μόνος διὰ τῆς ἀριστερᾶς ἀναιρῶν διὰ τῆς δεξιᾶς ζωοποιῆσαι δύναται, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ πατάξαι καὶ ἀναστῆσαι κείμενον.

διὰ τοῦτο πρῶτον ὑπὸ τοῦ προδρόμου Σίμωνος προαπατηθέντες, θεῷ τὰς ψυχὰς ἀπεθάνετε καὶ τὰ σώματα ἐπατάχθητε· δύνασθε δὲ ὁμοίως τὸ δεύτερον, διὰ τῆς μετανοίας (ὡς ἔφην) τὰ θεῷ ἀρέσκοντα ἀναδεξάμενοι καὶ τὰ σώματα ἀναρρῶσαι καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἀναλαβεῖν. ἔστιν δὲ τὰ ἀρέσκοντα τῷ θεῷ τὸ αὐτῷ προσεύχεσθαι, αὐτὸν αἰτεῖν ὡς πάντα νόμῳ κριτικῷ διδόντα, „τραπέζης δαιμόνων“ ἀπέχεσθαι, νεκρᾶς μὴ γεύεσθαι σαρκός, μὴ ψαύειν αἵματος, ἐκ παντὸς ἀπολούεσθαι λύματος. τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ ἐνὶ λόγῳ ὡς οἱ θεὸν σέβοντες ἤκουσαν Ἰουδαῖοι, καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀκούσατε ἅπαντες, ἐν πολλοῖς σώμασιν μίαν γνώμην ἀναλαβόντες Ἅπερ ἕκαστος ἑαυτῷ βούλεται καλά, τὰ αὐτὰ βουλευέσθω καὶ τῷ πλησίον. οὕτω δ’ ἂν ὑμῶν ἕκαστος νοήσειεν τὸ καλόν, εἰ ἑαυτῷ διαλεχθείη τὰ τοιαῦτα Οὐ θέλεις φονευθῆναι, ἕτερον μὴ φονεύσῃς· οὐ θέλεις τὴν σὴν ὑφ’ ἑτέρου μοιχευθῆναι γυναῖκα, τὴν ἑτέρου μὴ μοίχευε γαμετήν· οὐ θέλεις τι τῶν σῶν κλαπῆναι, ἑτέρου μὴ κλέπτε μηδέν. καὶ οὕτως ἀφ’ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν τὸ εὔλογον συννοοῦντες καὶ ποιοῦντες, θεῷ προσφιλεῖς γενόμενοι, ἐπιτεύξεσθε τῆς ἰάσεως, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἐν τῷ παρόντι αἰῶνι βασανισθήσεσθε τὰ σώματα καὶ ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι κολασθήσεσθε τὰς ψυχάς.

τοιαῦτα ὑπὸ τοῦ Πέτρου ἐν ὀλίγαις ἡμέραις κατηχηθέντες καὶ ἰαθέντες ἐβαπτίσθησαν, ἔπειτα τοῖς λοιποῖς αὐτοῦ θαύμασιν περίλυποι πάντες ἐν μέσαις ταῖς ἀγοραῖς πανδημεὶ ἐπὶ σποδοῦ καὶ σάκκου ἐκαθέζοντο, μετανοοῦντες ἐπὶ τοῖς πρότερον ἡμαρτημένοις. καὶ οἱ ἐν Σιδῶνι ταῦτα ἀκούσαντες τὰ ὅμοια ἐποίησαν, καὶ ἱκέτας πρὸς τὸν Πέτρον ἀπέστελλον ὡς αὐτοὶ διὰ τὰς νόσους πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐλθεῖν μὴ δυνάμενοι. ὁ Πέτρος δὲ ἡμερῶν οὐ πολλῶν ἐνδιατρίψας τῇ Τύρῳ καὶ κατηχήσας τοὺς ἐν αὐτῇ ἅπαντας καὶ παντοδαπῶν αὐτοὺς ἀπαλλάξας παθῶν, ἐκκλησίαν τε συστησάμενος καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν ἑπομένων αὐτῷ πρεσβυτέρων ἐπίσκοπον αὐτοῖς καταστήσας ὥρμησεν εἰς Σιδῶνα. ὁ δὲ Σίμων μαθὼν ἥκοντα τὸν Πέτρον εὐθὺς ἀπέδρα εἰς Βηρυτὸν μετὰ Ἀππίωνος καὶ τῶν αὐτοῦ ἑταίρων.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.

passages.text: On the fourth day of our stay in Tyre, toward dawn, when Peter had come forward, not a few inhabitants of the neighboring places and very many from Tyre itself met him and cried out, saying, “May God have mercy on us through you; may he heal us through you.” Peter stood on a certain high stone so that he could be seen by everyone and, after greeting them in accordance with the law that reveres God, began as follows:

lexical_decisions.chosen: of our stay in Tyre
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ἐπιδημία denotes a temporary residence or stay, not an epidemic or an official visitation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: toward dawn
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase locates the event near the approach of daybreak.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when Peter had come forward
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect participle presents Peter as having gone out or come forward; “come forward” fits his subsequent public address without specifying an unmentioned building.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after greeting them in accordance with the law that reveres God
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσαγορεύω means greet or address, while the dative θεοσεβεῖ νόμῳ expresses the God-revering rule or manner governing the greeting; “with a God-revering greeting” is also possible.

passages.text: God, who created heaven and the universe, does not lack an occasion for the salvation of those who wish to be saved. Therefore, no one should rashly accuse him of lacking benevolence toward humanity, even on account of things that appear bad. For the outcomes of what happens to a human being are unknown to humans and are suspected of tending toward evil, but they are known to God as things that will turn out well. Take Simon as an immediate example: being God’s left-hand power and holding authority over those who do not know God for the purpose of doing harm, he was able to surround you with diseases. These diseases, having been permitted to arise through God’s good providence, compelled you, after you had looked around for and found the one able to heal, to accept, on the pretext of treatment of the body, the things that seem good to God and to be persuaded to set your minds on them, so that in this way, together with your bodies that are to be saved, you might also have your souls safe.

lexical_decisions.chosen: does not lack an occasion for the salvation
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Occasion” preserves πρόφασις as grounds or an opportunity for action and also makes visible its lexical connection with the later προφάσει. In the later occurrence, bodily treatment is the ostensible basis on which the hearers accept divine instruction, so the context supports the more pointed rendering “pretext” there.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅθεν μηδὲ ἐπὶ τοῖς δοκοῦσιν φαύλοις ὑπὸ προπετείας τις αὐτὸν ὡς μὴ φιλάνθρωπον αἰτιάσθω
lexical_decisions.chosen: Therefore, no one should rashly accuse him of lacking benevolence toward humanity, even on account of things that appear bad
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering treats ὑπὸ προπετείας as the rash manner or impulse behind the accusation and preserves the emphatic force of μηδέ with “even.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: of lacking benevolence toward humanity
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιλάνθρωπος describes one who is humane or benevolent toward people; the rendering preserves the negation without importing a specialized theological title.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτίκα γοῦν Σίμων ἀριστερὰ τοῦ θεοῦ δύναμις ὢν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Take Simon as an immediate example: being God’s left-hand power
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτίκα γοῦν introduces a concrete immediate example, and ἀριστερὰ τοῦ θεοῦ δύναμις directly identifies Simon as the left-hand power of God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν τὸν θεὸν οὐκ εἰδότων ἐπὶ κακοποιΐᾳ τὴν ἐξουσίαν ἔχων
lexical_decisions.chosen: holding authority over those who do not know God for the purpose of doing harm
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive marks those over whom the authority operates, while ἐπὶ κακοποιΐᾳ states its harmful purpose or function.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on the pretext of treatment of the body
lexical_decisions.rationale: This repeats the πρόφασις wording used earlier. Here bodily healing functions as the ostensible basis or occasion for accepting what pleases God; “on the occasion of bodily treatment” is possible, but “on the pretext” better preserves the distinction between the immediate bodily aim and the further saving outcome.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ θεῷ δοκοῦντα ἀναδεξαμένους πεισθῆναι φρονεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to accept the things that seem good to God and to be persuaded to set your minds on them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle describes accepting what is pleasing to God, followed by persuasion in thought. More literally, the final words can be rendered “to be persuaded to think,” but English benefits from making the contextually supplied object explicit.

passages.text: I learn, then, that after sacrificing an ox he gave you a feast in the middle of the marketplace, and that in this way, carried away by much wine, you joined the evil demons in showing hospitality to their ruler. Thus most of you were seized by afflictions, because in ignorance you drew against yourselves, with your own hands, the sword of destruction. For the demons would not have had authority against you if you had not first shared a meal with their ruler. From the beginning, God, who created everything, laid down this law for the two rulers in every instance—the ruler of the right and the ruler of the left: neither of them is to have authority unless he first becomes the table companion of someone whom he wishes to benefit or harm. As, then, by partaking of the sacrifices dedicated to demons you were enslaved to the leader of evil, so, if you cease from these things and take refuge in God through the good, right-hand leader, honoring him without sacrifice by doing what he wishes, know well that along with the healing of the body you will also have healthy souls. For he alone, destroying through the left hand, can give life through the right hand; likewise, he can both strike and raise up one who lies fallen.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that after sacrificing an ox he gave you a feast
lexical_decisions.rationale: βουθυτέω denotes sacrificing an ox or cattle. The unexpressed subject is most naturally Simon from the preceding context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἅμα τοῖς πονηροῖς δαίμοσιν τὸν ἄρχοντα αὐτῶν ἐφιλοφρονεῖσθε
lexical_decisions.chosen: you joined the evil demons in showing hospitality to their ruler
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιλοφρονέομαι can mean welcome, entertain, or treat graciously. “Showing hospitality” preserves the banquet setting, though “paying court to” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you had first shared a meal
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁμοδίαιτος can describe living or dining together. The surrounding references to sacrifices and table fellowship support the meal-related rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δυσὶν ἑκάστοτε ἄρχουσι, δεξιῶν τε καὶ εὐωνύμων
lexical_decisions.chosen: for the two rulers in every instance—the ruler of the right and the ruler of the left
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἑκάστοτε indicates each recurring instance, while the genitives distinguish the right-hand and left-hand sides or powers. “For each pair of rulers, of right and left” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: honoring him without sacrifice by doing what he wishes
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀθύτοις describes honors not involving sacrifice. The rendering takes doing what God wishes as the form of those non-sacrificial honors.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὸς γὰρ μόνος διὰ τῆς ἀριστερᾶς ἀναιρῶν διὰ τῆς δεξιᾶς ζωοποιῆσαι δύναται
lexical_decisions.chosen: For he alone, destroying through the left hand, can give life through the right hand
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle ἀναιρῶν describes destruction through the left, while the infinitive ζωοποιῆσαι with δύναται states his ability to give life through the right.

source_issues.issue: An isolated raised point is printed immediately before ἀθύτοις despite the preceding comma. It appears to be stray or redundant punctuation and contributes no lexical content; that interpretation remains provisional.

passages.text: For this reason, after first being deceived by Simon the forerunner, you died to God in your souls, and your bodies were struck. But in the same way you can, a second time, through reorientation—as I said—accept the things pleasing to God and both restore your bodies to health and recover your souls. What pleases God is this: to pray to him; to make requests of him as the one who gives everything according to a judicial law; to abstain from “the table of demons”; not to taste dead flesh; not to touch blood; and to wash oneself clean of every pollution. As for the rest, hear it, all of you, in one saying, just as the Jews who revere God have heard it, taking up one mind in many bodies: “Whatever good things each person wants for himself, he should plan the same things for his neighbor as well.” Each of you would understand what is good in this way, if he were to reason with himself as follows: “You do not want to be murdered; do not murder another. You do not want another to commit adultery with your wife; do not commit adultery with another man’s wedded wife. You do not want any of your possessions to be stolen; do not steal anything belonging to another.” And so, recognizing from your own case what is reasonable and doing it, you will become dear to God and obtain healing; for otherwise you will be tormented in your bodies in the present age and punished in your souls in the age to come.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after first being deceived by Simon the forerunner
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόδρομος explicitly calls Simon a forerunner, while προαπατάω presents the deception as prior; the translation does not specify whose forerunner he is.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through reorientation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context concerns moral and spiritual redirection expressed by accepting what pleases God. “Through repentance” is the traditional alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τὰ σώματα ἀναρρῶσαι καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἀναλαβεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: both restore your bodies to health and recover your souls
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀναρρωννύω denotes renewed bodily strength, while ἀναλαμβάνω here presents the souls as regained or recovered; “take up your souls again” would be more formally literal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὸν αἰτεῖν ὡς πάντα νόμῳ κριτικῷ διδόντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: to make requests of him as the one who gives everything according to a judicial law
lexical_decisions.rationale: κριτικός can mean discriminating or judicial. “According to a law of discernment” is possible, but the surrounding emphasis on consequences and punishment favors “judicial.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: not to taste dead flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording directly prohibits tasting flesh that is dead; it has not been generalized to a familiar dietary formula.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν πολλοῖς σώμασιν μίαν γνώμην ἀναλαβόντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: taking up one mind in many bodies
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the author’s image of bodily plurality united in a single judgment or disposition.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ θέλεις τὴν σὴν ὑφ’ ἑτέρου μοιχευθῆναι γυναῖκα, τὴν ἑτέρου μὴ μοίχευε γαμετήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: You do not want another to commit adultery with your wife; do not commit adultery with another man’s wedded wife
lexical_decisions.rationale: The English changes the first clause from passive to active to avoid implying sexual coercion while preserving the participants and the repeated adultery terminology. The distinction between γυναῖκα, “wife,” and γαμετήν, “wedded wife,” is also retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπεὶ καὶ ἐν τῷ παρόντι αἰῶνι βασανισθήσεσθε
lexical_decisions.chosen: for otherwise you will be tormented in your bodies in the present age
lexical_decisions.rationale: After an exhortation or stated favorable outcome, ἐπεί can introduce the consequence that follows otherwise. The formally possible “since indeed you will be tormented” would obscure the warning contrast supplied by the context.

passages.text: After being instructed in such things by Peter over a few days and being healed, they were baptized. Then, all deeply grieved by his further wonders, they sat together as a whole populace in the middle of the marketplaces on ashes and sackcloth, reorienting themselves over the sins they had previously committed. When those in Sidon heard these things, they did the same and sent suppliants to Peter, since they themselves were unable to come to him because of their diseases. Peter, after staying in Tyre for not many days, instructing everyone in it, freeing them from every kind of affliction, forming a church, and appointing for them a bishop from among the elders who followed him, set out for Sidon. On learning that Peter was coming, Simon immediately fled to Beirut with Appion and his companions.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοιαῦτα ὑπὸ τοῦ Πέτρου ἐν ὀλίγαις ἡμέραις κατηχηθέντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: After being instructed in such things by Peter over a few days
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατηχέω here means to instruct orally; “catechized” would preserve the later technical term but would be less accessible in modern English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: deeply grieved by his further wonders
lexical_decisions.rationale: περίλυπος takes the dative as the cause or occasion of grief, and λοιπός can mean remaining, other, or further. “Deeply grieved at his other wonders” is a close alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πανδημεὶ ἐπὶ σποδοῦ καὶ σάκκου ἐκαθέζοντο
lexical_decisions.chosen: they sat together as a whole populace ... on ashes and sackcloth
lexical_decisions.rationale: πανδημεί means collectively or with the whole populace, while ἐπί with the genitive presents ashes and sackcloth as what they sat upon.

lexical_decisions.chosen: reorienting themselves over the sins they had previously committed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle describes moral reorientation in response to earlier sins, while ἐπί identifies those sins as its occasion. “Repenting over their former sins” is the traditional alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: forming a church
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the context of appointing a bishop from among elders, ἐκκλησία denotes an organized congregation or church, and συνίστημι denotes forming or establishing it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: On learning that Peter was coming
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the narrative sequence Peter has just set out for Sidon, so the present participle is best understood as his approach. Because ἥκω can also have a perfect-like sense, “had arrived” remains grammatically possible.

"translation_policy_text": "# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
